summary: Trimethoprim is a synthetic folate-antagonist antibacterial that inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. As monotherapy (distinct from the co-trimoxazole combination) it is indicated for the treatment of initial episodes of uncomplicated urinary tract infections due to susceptible organisms such as Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter species, and coagulase-negative staphylococci including Staphylococcus saprophyticus. The usual adult oral dose is 100 mg every 12 hours or 200 mg every 24 hours for 10 days. It is renally cleared and requires dose reduction in moderate renal impairment (and is not recommended if CLcr <15 mL/min). As a folate antagonist it can cause megaloblastic anaemia and other blood dyscrasias, and it is contraindicated in megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency. It commonly raises serum potassium (acting like a potassium-sparing diuretic on the distal nephron) and should be used cautiously with other agents that raise potassium. It should be avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy because of folate antagonism.
indications: Treatment of initial episodes of uncomplicated urinary tract infections due to susceptible strains of E. coli, P. mirabilis, K. pneumoniae, Enterobacter species, and coagulase-negative staphylococci (including S. saprophyticus)

dosage.d: 100 mg every 12 hours OR 200 mg every 24 hours, each for 10 days
dosage.t: Use only for proven or strongly suspected susceptible infection

admin: Take with a full glass of water; may be taken with or without food
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
Use only to treat infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria (limit resistance)
Reduce dose in moderate renal impairment; do not use if CLcr <15 mL/min
moa: Trimethoprim blocks the production of tetrahydrofolic acid from dihydrofolic acid by binding to and reversibly inhibiting the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase. This binding is far stronger for the bacterial enzyme than for the corresponding mammalian enzyme, giving selective toxicity. By depleting tetrahydrofolate, trimethoprim blocks the synthesis of thymidine and bacterial nucleic acids and proteins. When combined with sulfamethoxazole (in co-trimoxazole), the two agents block sequential steps in the folate pathway, but trimethoprim alone is bacteriostatic to bactericidal against susceptible urinary pathogens.

absolute: Documented megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency
relative: Possible folate deficiency (elderly, malnourished, chronic alcoholism, anticonvulsant therapy, malabsorption)
Significant renal impairment (CLcr <15 mL/min - not recommended)
Risk factors for hyperkalaemia (renal impairment, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics)
monitor: Complete blood count, especially with high doses or prolonged use
Signs of blood disorders (sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura)

preg: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and crosses the placenta. Some epidemiologic studies suggest an association with congenital malformations (particularly neural tube defects) when used in early pregnancy. It should be avoided in the first trimester; if used later in pregnancy when benefits outweigh risks, folic acid supplementation is advisable. Use only if clearly needed and after discussion of risks.
lact: Trimethoprim is excreted in human milk. The amounts ingested by a breastfed infant are small and it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding of healthy term infants. Caution is advised in premature, jaundiced, ill, or G6PD-deficient infants. Monitor the infant for possible effects.
renal: Trimethoprim is eliminated primarily by the kidneys. For creatinine clearance of 15 to 30 mL/min the dose should be reduced to 50 mg every 12 hours. Use in patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 15 mL/min is not recommended. Renal impairment also increases the risk of hyperkalaemia.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with marked hepatic impairment. There is no specific labelled dose adjustment, but impaired metabolism and the risk of haematologic toxicity warrant care.

major: Potassium-raising drugs - ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride), potassium supplements (additive hyperkalaemia, can be severe)
Other folate antagonists, e.g. methotrexate (additive bone marrow suppression / megaloblastic anaemia)
Phenytoin (trimethoprim inhibits its metabolism - increased phenytoin levels/toxicity)
moderate: Oral anticoagulants such as warfarin (enhanced anticoagulant effect)
Dofetilide and other drugs cleared by renal cation transport (raised levels - trimethoprim inhibits OCT2/renal tubular secretion)
Digoxin (possible increased serum levels, especially in the elderly)
minor: May reduce tubular secretion of creatinine, raising measured serum creatinine without a true fall in GFR
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with trimethoprim alone
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause artefactual elevation of serum creatinine (blocks tubular secretion) and may interfere with serum methotrexate assays; can raise serum potassium

serious: Megaloblastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, neutropenia, methaemoglobinaemia
Severe hyperkalaemia (especially with other potassium-raising drugs or renal impairment)
Severe hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (rare)

monitoring: Serum potassium, particularly in renal impairment or with other potassium-raising drugs
Complete blood count with prolonged or high-dose therapy, or if signs of a blood disorder appear (sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura)
Renal function (creatinine, with the caveat that trimethoprim raises measured creatinine)
Signs of serious skin reaction or diarrhoea
counsel: Take the full course exactly as prescribed, even once you feel better, and drink plenty of fluids
Tell your doctor about kidney problems or any medicines for blood pressure or potassium - this drug can raise potassium
Report sore throat, fever, unusual bruising or paleness, which can signal a blood problem
Stop and seek urgent care for any spreading rash, blistering, or mouth/eye sores
Report severe or bloody diarrhoea, even weeks after finishing the course
Tell your doctor if you are or may become pregnant - it is best avoided in early pregnancy
pk: Well absorbed orally; antibacterial activity within hours of dosing
Peak serum concentration about 1 to 4 hours after an oral dose
Approximately 8 to 10 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Supports twice-daily or once-daily dosing; high urinary concentrations
Store at controlled room temperature (about 20-25 degrees C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Trimethoprim causes hyperkalaemia by blocking the epithelial sodium channel in the distal nephron (acting like amiloride) - watch potassium, especially with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, or renal impairment.
As a folate antagonist it can cause megaloblastic anaemia and is contraindicated in folate-deficiency megaloblastic anaemia.
It raises measured serum creatinine by inhibiting tubular creatinine secretion without truly lowering GFR.
Avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy; supplement folic acid if used later when benefits outweigh risks.
Renal dosing: 50 mg q12h for CLcr 15-30 mL/min; not recommended below 15 mL/min.
It inhibits phenytoin metabolism and can potentiate warfarin and sulfonylureas/repaglinide.
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule - do not take a double dose to make up. Finish the whole course as prescribed.
overdose: Acute overdose (ingestion of 1 gram or more) may cause nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, mental depression, confusion, and bone marrow depression. Treatment is gastric lavage and general supportive measures; acidification of the urine increases renal elimination of trimethoprim. Peritoneal dialysis is not effective and haemodialysis is only moderately effective. Chronic high-dose use can cause bone marrow depression (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, megaloblastic anaemia) - discontinue and give leucovorin (folinic acid) 5 to 15 mg daily until haematologic recovery.
